People with lots of friends, how do you maintain all of your relationships?

i invite certain groups to certain things i do. i tried to invite all my friends to my bday party once a couple years ago and about 60 people showed up and they all segregated into small groups, was very awkward.

It's a lot of time investment, and it's completely worth it. If I get invited and can't make it, I let them know; I don't ignore anything. I do my best to make all the important things like birthdays, anniversaries, etc. And if someone needs help, I try my best to be there for him/her. I chat a lot online too with everyone and make sure to message friends I haven't seen in a while.

I used to call it "doing the rounds". Every, say Thursday I would make a mental map of the 8 or 10 people that I considered friends, then I would spend 20 min with each before heading in to the next stop. It was just enough time to catch up and not wear out my welcome.

It was a lot of work and time invested for me. I felt like I had to keep track of everyone and make it a point to hang out with them every few days. I would cycle through my friends list to ensure I made time for everyone during the month.

I got tired of doing this and just maintained my relationships with my close friends and let everyone else go. I still say hi to them when I see them online but never to the point where I'm juggling different groups of friends.

I'm really good about introducing friends to each other. I don't introduce everyone to everyone, I'm strategic about it.

I'm actually a little too good at it. I introduced my ex girlfriend to her current husband. I introduced my two good friends to each other and they became best friends; nowadays I'm the outsider. I also keep touch with people even if I haven't physically seen them for months. The best way m, I think, is bull shit Facebook conversations that we just go back and forth on.

Prior to having kids, it was super easy. Mostly, it was owed to the fact that my wife and I were able to go out a lot and everybody typically went to the same 5 or 6 places. Maintaining the relationships is mostly just about having the time and making the time to go out and interact.

Maintaining good friendships shouldn't require crazy effort. Of course, you need to invest time in your friends but you also have to give folks the benefit of the doubt that when they can't make it, they can't for a good reason. All the friends I have give each other the benefit of the doubt and during our man periods, we reach out and get more information before passing judgement. It's amazing what being an adult about things can do.

Hi /v/coffee guys!

I'm looking for feedback / experience sharing about the process of choosing a grinder.

I was reading some reviews about coffee grinders (mostly manual ones), and the feedbacks are often that the different pieces have some play that make the whole thing more fragile, or that force you to reset the grinding size quite often. It's so hard to choose one without having personnaly tested it beforehand!

Anyway, I thought I might ask you to share about your own grinders :)

These questions are here to guide the conversation, but please feel free to answer and contribute as you wish.

  • What grinder did you choose?
  • How much did it cost?
  • How often do you use it?
  • With which brewing method(s)?
  • What makes it a good product?
  • If you had to choose a different one today, what grinder would you get? (and why?)
How did you choose your coffee grinder?

I didn't choose a grinder. The grinder chose me. which is my overly-pretentious way of saying that it was a gift. :)

But I use it on a daily basis for both espresso and press pot.

What makes it a good product? It grinds coffee. Not being snarky here. It does what I need it to do, and has done so for so long that I no longer remember who gave it to me or why. But it's still grinding coffee.
A coffee grinder is a neat gift idea! Could you tell us which model it is (automatic/manual + brand?) and how long you've been using it?
I made a mental note to check when I got home, and then forgot. As for how long, the best I can tell you is long enough that I've forgotten how long. Which says a lot about reliability, I think.

The Lido 2 is the best, cheapest grinder. About $190. It is ridiculously good for every brew method. I prefer it to all of the grinders at my shop. It easily rivals and beats the Baratza Vario and Forte. It's incredible how expensive the motor mechanism makes grinders

I fantasize about getting one and I keep seeing reviews like yours, that leave me with no doubt that it's a good decision. 190$ is an investment I'm not ready to make yet, but if it's one of these products you buy once for life, it seems like it's worth it.

It really depends on what sort of brewing you enjoy

If you brew filtered coffee most of the time (French press/plunger, drip coffee, Swiss-gold, chemex etc.), you really don't need to buy an expensive grinder, which does a fantastic job at super fine grinding.

But if you're using an espresso machine, you'd better be ready to spend a bit of money to buy a decent grinder.

Anyway, I personally find this pretty handy :) (Hario Skerton hand grinder) http://coffeegeek.com/reviews/grinders/harioskerton

I personally own one and it's pretty decent. It does a phenomenal job at producing both find ground for espresso and medium ground for filtered coffee.

It's about ~$30 USD on Amazon (I live in NZ and paid much more :( not very happy about that).

I've been using it between 2~3 times a day for last two years.

I make medium-fine ground for filtered coffee (Swiss Gold, V60, and Syphon) and fine ground for Presso mechanical espresso machine at work.

There are many good things I can comment on about this thing: It's cheap. It is very versatile (you can make both coarse and fine ground that are quality as). And because it's a hand grinder, you can have a unique experience of grinding your own coffee!

The only draw back is that when you make medium ground, it can be inconsistent. However, you can fix that by purchasing a lower bearing. http://www.shapeways.com/product/JLU2RCSZY/hario-skerton-coffee-grinder-bottom-bracket http://www.orphanespresso.com/OE-Lower-Bearing-UPGRADE-KIT-for-Hario-Skerton-Kyocera-CM50-Hand-Grinders_p_4066.html

Unless I was given a large sum of money to replace my grinder, I'm not thinking about changing it. There's no decent grinder around up to ~$250USD that does a pretty decent job like this one does, including the machine grinders. As for hand grinder, I think this one is nonpareil.

I have seen this grinder in action and it apparently does a good job, however I'm afraid it can be quite long if you need to prepare coffee for several persons. Do you usually grind just for yourself, or are you preparing more?

Yes, I use it mostly for myself. But It doesn't take long to grind beans for more people. Plus, you can make other people to grind it or pass it around! But if it is a daily routine, it might be wiser to look at other options.
